source.text:
--- Page 1 ---
Harbour Retail — Junior Data Analyst Demo JD 
Junior Data Analyst 
Company: Harbour Retail 
Location: Sydney, NSW 
Employment Type: Full-time 
Experience Level: Entry Level / Junior 
Team: Data & Analytics 
About Harbour Retail 
Harbour Retail is a growing Sydney-based e-commerce startup using data to improve 
customer acquisition, digital shopping experiences and commercial performance. 
As the business grows, we are looking for a Junior Data Analyst to support the team in 
turning website marketing and sales data into clear insights that help teams make 
better decisions. 
You will work with members of the Data, Marketing and Commercial teams and will be 
supported by more experienced analysts. This role is suited to a recent graduate or 
early-career analyst who enjoys working with data, investigating business questions and 
communicating findings clearly. 
About the Role 
As a Junior Data Analyst, you will help collect, validate, analyses and interpret business 
data across website traffic, marketing channels and online sales. 
Your work will include routine reporting as well as ad hoc investigations into changes in 
business performance. 
A key part of the role is not only calculating metrics, but understanding what those 
metrics mean, identifying when further evidence is required, and communicating 
findings to non-technical stakeholders. 
Key Responsibilities 
Data Preparation and Quality 
• Collect, organize and validate data from sales, website and marketing sources. 
• Check datasets for missing values, inconsistencies and obvious data-quality 
issues. 
• Maintain clear documentation of data sources, calculations and analytical 
assumptions. 
• Support reliable and consistent reporting across business teams. 
SQL and Data Analysis 

--- Page 2 ---
• Write basic SQL queries to extract, filter, group and summaries business data. 
• Use aggregation techniques to analyses performance across products, time 
periods and acquisition channels. 
• Calculate and monitor key business metrics such as website traffic, orders and 
conversion rates. 
• Compare results across periods or customer/channel segments to identify 
meaningful changes. 
Business Analysis and Problem Solving 
• Investigate changes in business performance and identify possible explanations 
supported by available data. 
• Distinguish between what the data directly shows and what remains uncertain. 
• Identify when additional data is required before reaching a business conclusion. 
• Perform ad hoc analysis to support questions raised by Marketing, Product or 
Commercial teams. 
• Translate analytical findings into practical next steps or recommendations where 
the available evidence supports them. 
Reporting and Visualization 
• Assist in creating recurring reports, tables and dashboards using Excel or 
business-intelligence tools. 
• Present metrics and analytical findings in a clear, structured and accessible 
format. 
• Support the development of simple visualizations that help stakeholders 
understand trends and performance. 
Stakeholder Communication 
• Explain analytical findings clearly to colleagues who may not have a technical 
background. 
• Summaries the business implications of an analysis rather than only presenting 
calculations. 
• Clearly communicate assumptions, limitations and areas where further 
investigation is required. 
• Collaborate with cross-functional teams to understand business questions and 
data requirements. 
Skills and Experience 

--- Page 3 ---
Essential 
• Bachelor’s degree, or near completion, in Data Analytics, Business Analytics, 
Statistics, Mathematics, Computer Science, Economics or a related discipline. 
• Foundational knowledge of SQL, including filtering, grouping and basic 
aggregation. 
• Strong Excel or spreadsheet skills. 
• Ability to calculate and interpret basic business metrics. 
• Strong analytical and structured problem-solving skills. 
• High attention to detail and commitment to data accuracy. 
• Ability to explain analytical findings clearly in written and verbal form. 
• Willingness to learn and work in a fast-moving startup environment. 
Desirable 
• Internship, university project or portfolio experience involving data analysis. 
• Familiarity with Python or R. 
• Exposure to Power BI, Tableau or another data-visualization platform. 
• Basic understanding of digital analytics, e-commerce or marketing performance 
metrics. 
• Experience presenting analytical work to non-technical audiences. 
What Good Looks Like in This Role 
A successful Junior Data Analyst does more than produce correct calculations. 
You should be able to: 
• identify the right metric for a business question; 
• analyses data accurately; 
• recognize when a conclusion is or is not supported by the available evidence; 
• explain your reasoning clearly; 
• identify what additional information may be required; and 
• turn analysis into a sensible next step for the business. 
Example Business Questions You May Work On 
• Why has website conversion changed even though traffic has increased? 
• Which acquisition channels appear to be driving changes in customer behavior? 

--- Page 4 ---
• Does the available evidence support changing marketing investment? 
• What additional information would be needed before recommending a 
commercial action? 
• How should an analytical finding be explained to a Marketing Manager or other 
non-technical stakeholder? 
Tools 
You may work with: 
• SQL 
• Microsoft Excel / Google Sheets 
• Power BI or similar BI tools 
• Basic Python or R where appropriate 
• Website, marketing and sales datasets 
What We Value 
We value candidates who are curious, evidence-driven and comfortable saying when 
the available data is not sufficient to support a conclusion. 
For a junior role, we do not expect you to know everything. We are interested in how 
you approach a problem, how carefully you work with evidence, and how clearly you 
explain your reasoning.

marks.meaning: Fully supports the observable requirement with relevant explanations and boundaries.
Mostly supports the requirement; the rationale identifies a specific non-critical gap.
Partially supports the requirement, with a material gap affecting interpretation.
A relevant attempt is visible but specific support is weaker than the mark-2 anchor.
A clear, observed problem is supported by the source text; not a substitute for missing evidence.
Not enough evidence to judge. Record the checked scope; never convert this to zero.

criteria.title: Query grain, aggregation and joins
criteria.observableSupport: Input grain is clear and aggregation or joins answer the stated question without visible double counting. A join is not required when the question does not need one.

anchors.0: A visibly duplicating join produces incorrect key counts that are presented as correct.
anchors.2: Readable basic aggregation, but the grain or counting effect of a join is insufficiently explained.
anchors.4: Clear grain and appropriate aggregation or joins, with duplicate-counting risk checked.

criteria.title: Time or group comparison and query traceability
criteria.observableSupport: The reporting windows and comparison groups are explicit and consistent with the query. Complexity earns no extra credit.

anchors.0: Different periods or unrelated groups are incorrectly treated as the same comparison.
anchors.2: A query or period comparison is present, but filters or boundary explanations are incomplete.
anchors.4: Windows, groups and comparison objects are clear; code and explanation support a reproducible comparison.

criteria.title: Validation and relevant edge cases
criteria.observableSupport: Inspect proposed checks or examples for relevant duplicates, missing values, zero denominators and boundaries. Static review does not establish execution.

anchors.0: The source claims correctness despite a known failed check, or uses a clearly invalid validation method.
anchors.2: Checks such as missing values or duplicates are mentioned, but methods or expected results are incomplete.
anchors.4: Actionable checks cover relevant boundaries and state expected results.

criteria.title: Metrics, denominators, units and calculations
criteria.observableSupport: Numerators, denominators, windows and units agree; calculations are reproducible and percentages are distinguished from percentage points where relevant.

anchors.0: A wrong denominator drives the main conclusion and is neither identified nor corrected.
anchors.2: The main calculation is usable but a relevant definition or unit is insufficiently explained.
anchors.4: Metric definitions, denominators, units, periods and calculations are clear and consistent.

criteria.title: Meaningful period or group comparisons
criteria.observableSupport: Compare appropriate periods or groups beyond repeating totals; consider weights and overlapping populations when applicable.

anchors.0: Overlapping populations are added or rates are directly averaged to produce a key conclusion.
anchors.2: One useful change is visible, but a relevant breakdown or baseline is missing.
anchors.4: Totals and relevant groups are compared appropriately, considering weights and overlapping populations.

criteria.title: Reproducibility, sources and limitations
criteria.observableSupport: Show the calculation process, missing information and scope. Presentation quality alone does not establish analytical correctness.

anchors.0: Information absent from the materials is used as an observed fact.
anchors.2: A process or limitation is described, but the other aspect is weak.
anchors.4: Reproducible working is supplied and missing data and scope are explicit.

criteria.title: Business question and decision framing
criteria.observableSupport: Connect the question to a practical business decision and realistic constraints at a junior analyst level; senior strategic ownership is not required.

anchors.0: An explicitly unrelated question is answered and used as the basis of the current decision.
anchors.2: A relevant change is described but its connection to a business decision is incomplete.
anchors.4: The business decision, question to answer and realistic constraints are clear.

criteria.title: Observations, hypotheses and causal claims
criteria.observableSupport: Separate observed facts, hypotheses and demonstrated causes, with appropriate inference limits.

anchors.0: A sole proven cause is explicitly asserted without corresponding evidence.
anchors.2: Hypothesis awareness is visible, but some statements still imply causation from association.
anchors.4: Facts and hypotheses are separate; plausible alternatives and inference limits are considered.

criteria.title: Evidence requests that distinguish explanations
criteria.observableSupport: Request relevant data and explain what different results would imply for competing explanations.

anchors.0: A circular or irrelevant method is explicitly presented as verifying the proposed explanation.
anchors.2: Specific additional data is requested, but how it distinguishes explanations is not explained.
anchors.4: Specific data, a comparison method and the contrasting implications are clear.

criteria.title: Practical next steps and validation
criteria.observableSupport: Propose an appropriate order, reason and way to check a practical next step; ask a senior colleague where decisions exceed the junior role.

anchors.0: The proposed action contradicts the source's own key evidence without explanation.
anchors.2: A relevant action exists but its sequence, validation measure or stopping condition is incomplete.
anchors.4: Priority, rationale, feasible steps and validation measures fit the stated constraints.

> Synthetic demo work sample, newly authored from the project scope described in the supplied fictional CV. It was not attached to the original CV. The figures and text below are demonstration material, not verified employment outcomes.

# Task Management Web Application: database note

## Scope
Companion to David's March-May 2026 university project. His CV names React, Node.js, Express, MySQL, login, task creation, status updates and basic search. The attached query illustrates the data-retrieval part of that scope, without adding a new analytics internship or unmentioned business project.

## Data contract and behaviour
A user can create many tasks. Each task has one creator ID and its own primary key. The task-list endpoint supplies the signed-in user's ID to the parameterised query. Status changes are handled by a separate endpoint; mutation code is not included here.

The join retrieves the creator display name; it should not multiply tasks. Proposed functional checks are listed beside the SQL. No run log, coverage percentage or performance benchmark is supplied.

## What this sample does and does not cover
The material shows a proposed application query and basic checking approach. It contains no period-over-period business comparison, conversion calculation, customer-behaviour investigation or business recommendation. The CV's software-development experience should not be relabelled as demonstrated data-analysis results.

-- SYNTHETIC DEMO WORK SAMPLE: Task Management Web Application.
-- Newly authored illustration of the university project in David Liu's fictional CV.
-- Static review only. This is application-data retrieval, not a completed analytics project.
-- users(id PRIMARY KEY, display_name)
-- tasks(id PRIMARY KEY, creator_id REFERENCES users(id), title, status, created_at)
-- tasks.status is one of: todo, in_progress, done.
-- One output row per task; users.id is unique, so this join is many-to-one.
-- Bind :current_user_id using the application driver's parameter mechanism.
SELECT t.id, t.title, t.status, t.created_at, u.display_name AS creator_name
FROM tasks AS t
LEFT JOIN users AS u ON u.id = t.creator_id
WHERE t.creator_id = :current_user_id
ORDER BY t.created_at DESC, t.id DESC;

-- Proposed functional checks (not recorded execution results):
-- A user with no tasks receives an empty result.
-- A task with a valid creator should appear once, not once per other task.
-- The returned task IDs should match the user's task IDs in the source table.
-- A missing display name should not remove a task from the result.
-- Access enforcement is checked separately in the authenticated API handler;
-- the named parameter itself is not proof that authorisation was implemented.

resources.content:
# Harbour Retail · Business context

Synthetic company task data, separate from every applicant's past project and not supplied by the JD. Product, campaign and investment details are demonstration assumptions, not JD company facts. Two consecutive, non-overlapping four-week windows use the same session and order definitions. No customer-level data is included.

Sessions rose from 1,000,000 to 1,180,000 (+18.00%). Conversion fell from 3.4% to 2.6%. Orders changed from 34,000 to 30,680 (-9.76%). Advertising spend rose from AUD 41739.13 to AUD 48000.00 (+15.00%).

New Paid Search campaigns launched at the start of the current period. The Spring Sale landing page also changed. These changes are possible explanations, not established causes. The business is considering increasing the advertising budget.

website_traffic.csv and orders.csv contain the same ten channel-period aggregates, not separate populations. channel_comparison.csv is a channel comparison, not individual campaign attribution. current_paid_search_devices.csv contains a current-period Paid Search device partition only: it reconciles to Paid Search but adds no new sessions. It contains no page-specific attribution or speed measurements. product_catalog.csv is context, not evidence of a conversion cause. Revenue uses a synthetic AUD 30 average order value; no order-level product attribution is implied.

Campaign × device × landing-page detail, historical device comparisons, load times and checkout events are still missing. Rates are derived from integer totals; displayed percentages round to two decimals. Do not average channel percentages or add overlapping resources. The chart compares whole four-week periods, not weekly trend points.

Investigate the strongest signals, separate observations from hypotheses, request discriminating evidence, and recommend a measured next step. No single prescribed conclusion or hiring decision is implied.

data-analysis.title: Conversion Metrics and Comparison
data-analysis.instructions: First consider an existing calculation or explanation that addresses the selected gap. Use harbour-retail-2026-09-v1 to define and calculate session, order and conversion changes across two four-week periods. Show numerators, denominators, units and a relevant group comparison with reproducible working. State overlapping populations and missing information. Submit calculation text and limitations, not an executable notebook. Do not invent page-speed measurements, weekly trends or historical device data.

business-problem-solving.title: Conversion Drop Investigation
business-problem-solving.instructions: First consider an existing explanation that addresses the selected gap. Investigate the conversion decline using harbour-retail-2026-09-v1. Distinguish observations from hypotheses, request evidence that could distinguish explanations, and recommend a practical next step with a way to check its result. Treat the 20-minute timebox as guidance, not a deadline. Work at a junior analyst level and identify decisions requiring an experienced colleague. Submit findings, hypotheses, missing evidence and next steps; incomplete work may still be reviewed.
